what_its_for: Nefazodone is an antidepressant used to treat depression. It helps improve your mood, energy level, appetite, and sleep, and reduces feelings of sadness, anxiety, and nervousness.
how_to_take: Take nefazodone by mouth, usually twice a day (in the morning and at night). You can take it with or without food. If it upsets your stomach, try taking it with a small snack. Swallow the tablet whole. Do not crush or chew it. Try to take it at the same times each day to help you remember.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a low dose, often 100 mg twice a day, and slowly increase it over time based on how you respond. The usual adult dose is between 300 mg and 600 mg per day split into two doses. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose and it is not almost time for your next dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is close to the time of your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not double up or take two doses at once to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store nefazodone at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. Do not use if past the expiration date.
what_to_avoid: Do not drink alcohol while taking nefazodone — it can increase drowsiness and dizziness. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery until you know how this medicine affects you. Do not take MAO inhibitors (such as phenelzine, tranylcypromine, or selegiline) at the same time or within 14 days of nefazodone. Avoid taking pimozide, carbamazepine, or certain cholesterol-lowering statin drugs (like simvastatin or lovastatin) with this medication. Grapefruit juice may interact with nefazodone — ask your pharmacist if this is a concern.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you notice: yellowing of your skin or eyes, dark urine, severe stomach pain, or extreme tiredness — these could be signs of serious liver problems. Call your doctor immediately if you have thoughts of suicide or self-harm, feel worse, or notice sudden mood changes. Also call if you experience confusion, rapid heartbeat, high fever, or unusual muscle stiffness (serotonin syndrome). Seek emergency care for any severe allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing. WARNING: Nefazodone has a rare but serious risk of liver failure. Report any sign of liver problems immediately.
when_it_works: Nefazodone does not work right away. Most people start to notice some improvement in sleep and appetite within the first 1 to 2 weeks. However, it may take 4 to 6 weeks or longer to feel the full benefit for your mood and depression. Keep taking it even if you do not feel better right away. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Older adults (65+): You may be started on a lower dose because this medication stays in the body longer. Be extra careful about dizziness and falls. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor before taking or stopping this medication if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Small amounts may pass into breast milk — discuss the risks and benefits with your doctor. Liver disease: Do NOT take nefazodone if you have liver problems or have had liver damage from this medication before. Children and teenagers: This medication is generally not recommended for patients under 18. All young patients starting antidepressants should be closely monitored for changes in mood or behavior.
